news.author: Funso Lawal
news.content:
Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) has turned AI chips and compute contracts into collateral for Wall Street credit. Lenders, including banks and asset managers, now finance computing infrastructure using equipment, customer contracts, and expected revenue as collateral.

On August 10, 2026, Nvidia announced partnerships with six institutions to establish financing platforms designed to mobilize more than $500 billion in third-party capital for AI infrastructure over time. The agreements were preliminary and subject to further development.

However, the financing model has moved beyond proposals. For instance, CoreWeave (CRWV) closed an $8.5 billion GPU-backed loan facility on March 31, 2026, while Lambda also closed a $926 million loan on August 27 and a $1.008 billion loan on October 1. 

Since AI infrastructure often requires billions of dollars in upfront spending, financing tied to contracted computing revenue gives lenders another funding source without relying solely on a company’s general corporate credit.

Key Takeaways

  • CoreWeave and Lambda secured billions in financing backed by AI infrastructure and customer contracts.
  • Nvidia’s partnerships with six major financial institutions aim to mobilize third-party capital, not guarantee a single $500 billion loan.
  • Customer defaults, falling GPU resale values, and weaker AI demand could leave lenders struggling to recover their money.

How GPU-Backed Credit Works

In a typical GPU-backed financing structure, a borrower raises debt to purchase or deploy AI servers and related infrastructure. A special-purpose vehicle may own the equipment and pledge it as collateral, while customer agreements provide the expected revenue used to repay the loan.

Some contracts require customers to pay for reserved capacity even when they do not use it fully. These take-or-pay terms can make revenue more predictable, but they do not eliminate customer default risk or guarantee that the borrower will cover operating costs.

Lenders therefore evaluate more than the hardware. They assess the customer’s creditworthiness, contract duration, expected utilization, electricity and maintenance costs, debt-service coverage, and the likely recovery value of the equipment after default.

The structure matters because a GPU fleet has two potential sources of credit support: cash generated by computing services and proceeds from selling the underlying assets. Both can weaken if AI demand falls or newer hardware makes older systems less competitive.

CoreWeave Sets The Benchmark

CoreWeave’s March 31 facility, known as DDTL 4.0, was structured as an $8.5 billion delayed-draw term loan to finance infrastructure supporting contracted cloud services. Moody’s assigned the facility an A3 rating, and Morningstar DBRS assigned it an A (low) rating.

The floating-rate tranche was priced at the secured overnight financing rate (SOFR) plus 2.25%, while its fixed-rate tranche carried financing costs of approximately 5.90%. The facility matures in March 2032 and is secured by substantially all assets of the borrowing entity.

The ratings revealed that a specific GPU-backed structure could reach investment-grade credit markets. They did not establish that GPU-backed loans generally carry investment-grade risk.

CoreWeave’s subsequent transactions illustrate the distinction:

The latter facilities carry different credit profiles and should not be compared on spread alone. Customer quality, contract duration, collateral coverage, financing structure, and market conditions can all affect pricing. A higher spread may compensate lenders for greater risk, but it does not establish that the expected return adequately covers potential losses.

Lambda Expands the Institutional Lending Market

The model is not limited to CoreWeave. On August 12, Lambda announced that it had priced a $926 million senior secured term loan B facility. 

The loan supported GPU infrastructure dedicated to an investment-grade customer and carried a Moody’s Baa2 rating. Pricing tightened to SOFR plus 3.00% during syndication.

On October 1, Lambda announced a separate $1 billion delayed-draw term loan with investment-grade ratings. It covers three customer deployments involving two investment-grade counterparties across multiple data centers.

These transactions show how lenders can finance infrastructure against contracted demand rather than relying exclusively on a company’s general corporate credit. They also highlight why customer credit quality and contract structure matter alongside the hardware.

Nvidia’s $500 Billion Financing Initiative

Nvidia’s August announcement expanded the model beyond individual borrowers. The company signed memorandums of understanding with Apollo Global Management (APO), BlackRock (BLK), Blackstone Inc. (BX), Brookfield Asset Management (BAM), Goldman Sachs (GS), and KKR & Co. Inc. (KKR) to develop independent financing platforms for customers across its AI ecosystem.

The goal is to mobilize more than $500 billion in third-party capital over time for supported platforms, not a single committed loan or a guarantee of future lending volumes.

Nvidia has a commercial interest in expanding the model. Financing can help customers acquire its systems without paying the full cost upfront, potentially supporting hardware sales and adoption of its CUDA software ecosystem. Meanwhile, institutions can finance AI infrastructure through debt and other investment structures.

Nvidia offers a residual value guarantee of up to 25%. This reduces losses if GPUs need to be remarketed, but it is transaction-specific and does not remove the need for lenders to underwrite customer and contract risk.

The scope, conditions, and beneficiaries of any support depend on the relevant agreements.

Who Benefits, and Who Carries the Risk?

Nvidia: Financing can broaden the pool of customers able to purchase its systems. However, greater financing activity does not guarantee stronger earnings if customers delay projects or AI demand weakens.

AI cloud providers: GPU-backed debt can fund infrastructure expansion without requiring the borrower to finance every purchase from existing cash. The trade-off is greater leverage and a need to generate enough operating cash flow to cover debt service.

Banks and institutional investors: These transactions create new lending opportunities and exposure to AI infrastructure. Returns depend on interest income, fees, default risk, collateral recovery, and the terms of each facility.

Enterprise customers: More financing can increase access to computing capacity. However, customers may face service disruption if a provider encounters financial distress, depending on contract protections and the availability of alternative providers.

Risks to Watch

1. Customer concentration: If a major customer defaults, reduces its computing commitments, or terminates a contract, the borrower may struggle to maintain the cash flow needed for debt service.

2. Technological obsolescence: Software upgrades can extend the useful life of installed Nvidia systems. However, new GPU generations can reduce the resale value and competitiveness of older hardware, weakening the collateral available to lenders.

3. Refinancing risk: When debt matures after the underlying customer contracts expire, lenders rely on renewals, replacement customers, or the resale value of the hardware. Lower utilization or weaker demand could reduce recovery values.

This reinforces the need to evaluate borrower-level leverage and cash flow rather than assuming that exposure to Nvidia hardware makes a loan safe.

Bottom Line

Nvidia GPUs are becoming more than computing equipment. Lenders use them as collateral to finance AI infrastructure, while contracts to supply computing power provide a potential source of loan repayments. 

CoreWeave and Lambda show that this model can attract billions of dollars in institutional credit, while Nvidia’s $500 billion financing initiative could expand it further.

However, GPU-backed loans are only as strong as the cash flow, customer contracts, and resale value supporting them. Older chips can lose value, customers can default, and providers can struggle to repay debt if demand weakens. 

For Wall Street, the opportunity is to earn returns from AI infrastructure lending. The real test is whether contracted revenue can cover the debt before the hardware loses too much value.

The AI boom powering Nvidia Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA) has entered its “manic phase,” Pulitzer Prize-winning historian Liaquat Ahamed warned Friday, comparing it to the railroad frenzy that ended in the Panic of 1873.

Speaking on the Prof G Markets podcast, Ahamed said competition, overbuilding and debt could undermine returns on the vast sums pouring into data centers, even if the boom continues another year or two.

When a Powerful Railroad Financier Ran Out of Money

Railroads transformed the economy, but many of the companies financing their expansion went bankrupt.

Ahamed traced the crash to Jay Cooke, a powerful banker who raised billions for the Union during the Civil War.

Cooke then backed the Northern Pacific, a new transcontinental railroad. With hundreds of miles of track laid, investors assumed he could finance the rest.

But in September 1873, Cooke announced he couldn’t secure the necessary funding. His firm collapsed, triggering a financial panic.

As Ahamed explained, if even Cooke couldn’t raise the money, what chance did smaller railroad companies have? Within three months, railroad construction had ground to a halt, and roughly a quarter of U.S. railroad companies defaulted within a year.

Ahamed drew a modern parallel: What if OpenAI suddenly couldn’t finance its enormous AI commitments? He later identified Oracle as another company potentially vulnerable to a funding crisis.

Why Nadella May Have Learned the Wrong Lesson

Microsoft Corp. (NASDAQ:MSFT) CEO Satya Nadella has cited Ahamed’s book on 1873, saying Microsoft would be careful not to overbuild.

Ahamed said Nadella “got the wrong end of the stick.” Individual railroad companies weren’t necessarily reckless. Each kept expanding because slowing down meant surrendering business to competitors.

“It’s the collectivity of their decisions that leads to overbuilding,” he said.

Today’s hyperscalers could face the same trap.

Nvidia’s Customers Face a Debt Test

Ahamed identified three warning signs before the railroad crash: excess capacity, eroding profitability and more expensive financing. He said much of today’s AI borrowing remains opaque.

He described Nvidia as “essentially lending to its customers,” although its arrangements also involve equity investments and purchase commitments rather than conventional loans.

Nvidia has invested in CoreWeave Inc. (NASDAQ:CRWV) and entered a $6.3 billion agreement to purchase qualifying unused computing capacity through 2032. Some CoreWeave bonds yielded around 16% this week amid mounting debt concerns.

Nvidia shares fell 1.8% Thursday amid the broader AI-stock selloff.

On Polymarket, traders put the probability of a defined AI downturn by Dec. 31 at roughly 7%. The contract requires at least three specified stress events.

That low probability is consistent with Ahamed’s view that the boom could run another year or two.

Financial crises, he noted, tend to “take much longer to happen than you imagined” before they “happen much faster than you thought they could.”

For the AI infrastructure boom, the winning formula was to borrow heavily in order to build quickly. That strategy backfired on CoreWeave Inc. (NASDAQ:CRWV). Shares fell 6.4% to $65.25 by 9:40 a.m. ET on Friday, putting the stock on track for a weekly loss of about 22%. A close at that level would be its lowest since May 2025.

CoreWeave’s five-year credit default swaps — contracts that insure investors against a missed debt payment — hit a record 1,194.5 basis points on Thursday, according to ICE Data Services data reported by Bloomberg.

That price implies a more than 60% chance of default within five years, by standard market calculations.

Its 9.75% notes due October 2031 slipped to 81.80 cents on the dollar on Friday, yielding 15.08%. Two months ago, the same bonds yielded about 12%.

Read Also: EXCLUSIVE: Is AI Growth Slowing Down? Memory Industry Expert Says It's 'Too Early' To Tell

Why Higher Rates Hit CoreWeave First

CoreWeave rents out Nvidia-powered computing capacity to AI developers. It buys the chips and builds the data centers before the rent arrives, and it borrows to fill the gap.

In the second quarter, it generated $679 million in operating cash flow while spending about $6.4 billion on equipment. Net interest expense more than doubled to $640 million.

That model worked when money was cheap.

On Friday, the 10-year Treasury yield rose 4 basis points to 5.12%. The 30-year rose 3 basis points to 5.45%, and the 2-year held at 4.76%.

Wednesday’s hotter-than-expected inflation report raised the odds of another Federal Reserve rate hike on Oct. 28. CoreWeave fell 15.5% that day.

‘Darwin Moment’

"Data centre bonds are having their Darwin moment, where the weakest credits struggle to survive," Ludovic Subran, chief investment officer at German insurer Allianz, told the Financial Times this week.

Rival neocloud Nebius Group N.V. (NASDAQ:NBIS) is down about 20% this week.

Bank of America’s Michael Hartnett sees the pressure moving up the food chain.

"We continue to lean risk-off next 3-4 weeks," the chief investment strategist said in his weekly Flow Show note.

He cited 3% inflation-adjusted yields, the Nov. 3 midterms and weak trading in AI "spenders and lenders."

The spenders are CoreWeave’s customers: Amazon, Alphabet, Meta, Microsoft and Oracle. The lenders include private credit firms, banks and bondholders.

Their AI spending is expected to reach $807 billion this year. As a result, their combined free cash flow is forecast to swing from $191 billion in 2025 to minus $63 billion this year, according to consensus estimates compiled by Bank of America.

Signal to Watch

"A rollover in semi prices signals further tightening of AI credit," Hartnett said, expecting an October Fed hike to restore credibility. Consumer prices have run above the Fed’s 2% target for 66 consecutive months.

In his view, a hike could pull long-term Treasury yields down another 20 basis points and limit losses in risky assets.

The question now is which companies can afford to finance the AI race at elevated interest rates.

Chip stocks just had their worst week in months, and Wall Street is asking whether the artificial-intelligence bubble is finally bursting.

A Bank of America analyst says the question comes too late. On valuations, the burst has already happened.

Vivek Arya told clients in a note dated Friday that Nvidia Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA), Broadcom Inc. (NASDAQ:AVGO) and Micron Technology Inc. (NASDAQ:MU) trade at about 13 times forward earnings on average.

That sits inside the 10-to-20 times range at which Cisco Systems Inc. (NASDAQ:CSCO) traded after the dot-com bubble burst.

"Investors are paying post-crash multiples for a cycle that hasn’t crashed," Arya said.

The Chip Sector Is Already In A Bear Market

The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index (SOX), which tracks the 30 largest U.S.-listed chip stocks, was down about 9% for the week by Friday morning and on track for an eighth straight daily decline.

The index — closely tracked by the Invesco PHLX Semiconductor ETF (NASDAQ:SOXQ) — now sits about 22% below its June 22 record close. A 20% drop from a peak is the usual definition of a bear market.

It is the second one this year. Between June 22 and July 29, the index lost 28.6% before rallying back.

Memory stocks took the heaviest hit. Micron fell 13.1% this week to around $894, after closing at a record $1,088 on Oct. 7.

Broadcom lost 6.5% and Nvidia 5.7%, while the S&P 500 slipped just 0.8%.

The selling started with memory.

Early in the week, Chinese memory maker CXMT announced plans for a server-memory product built on a new architecture that could pack in more storage, raising concerns that it could take market share from Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron.

Then inflation joined in.

A hotter-than-expected inflation reading on Wednesday revived worries about further Federal Reserve rate hikes and a higher cost of capital for the AI trade.

Collectively, 20 of the world’s most valuable AI and semiconductor stocks shed more than $1 trillion in market value through Thursday.

Read Also: Chip Meltdown Hits Micron, SanDisk and SK Hynix: $1 Trillion Vanishes From Memory Makers

This Is Not 2000, According to Bank of America

The dot-com bust left miles of fiber-optic cable unused, known as "dark fiber." Arya says AI hardware is the opposite. It runs near 100% utilization, and rental prices for older Nvidia chips launched between 2020 and 2024 are up 12% to 37% this year.

Rising prices for old equipment point to scarcity, not a glut.

Demand keeps climbing. Weekly usage on OpenRouter, a platform that routes requests to AI models, hit about 170 trillion tokens in early October, up from roughly 3 trillion a year ago. A token is a small chunk of text an AI model reads or writes.

Arya sees agentic AI, software that completes multi-step tasks on its own, as the next tenfold jump in computing demand.

Nvidia Is Bank of America’s Gigawatt Winner

With power and land now scarcer than chips, Arya expects spending to favor the most productive hardware. He argues that Nvidia captures more than 70% of AI system spending, backed by over $100 billion in announced buybacks.

Cloud and neocloud capital spending is expected to reach about $1.01 trillion in 2026, up 98%, and $1.39 trillion in 2027, up 37%.

Arya named three: a credit event at a neocloud, higher interest rates, and delays in power and permitting.

Neoclouds, such as CoreWeave Inc. (NASDAQ:CRWV) and Nebius Group N.V. (NASDAQ:NBIS), rent out AI computing capacity, often funded with debt.

The cash math is stretched.

Big cloud companies are expected to spend about 106.5% of their operating cash flow on capital projects in 2026.

The bank still sees that as sustainable, since the top five hyperscalers have raised about $382 billion this year, mostly in long-dated debt and equity.

Cisco shows how long a reset can last. Its stock peaked at $82 in March 2000, fell to $8.12 by October 2002, and didn’t reach that peak again until March 2026.

Bank of America bets that chip earnings, unlike Cisco’s, will keep growing.

Meta Platforms Inc. (NASDAQ:META) could deliver stronger-than-expected third-quarter revenue as artificial intelligence improves its advertising business, according to Bank of America.

In a Friday note, Bank of America Securities analyst Justin Post reiterated a Buy rating on Meta with an unchanged $810 price forecast.

The forecast implies approximately 10% upside from the stock’s reference price of $736.72.

Strong Advertising Demand Could Drive Earnings Beat

Post expects Meta to report third-quarter revenue of $63.8 billion, above Wall Street’s consensus estimate of $63.3 billion.

The analyst projects advertising revenue of $62.2 billion, representing 24% year-over-year growth.

Bank of America’s advertising checks suggest that AI-powered targeting and automation are helping advertisers generate stronger returns. These improvements could support continued revenue growth.

However, the firm lowered its third-quarter earnings estimate from $7.08 to $3.79 per share, below Wall Street’s $6.08 consensus.

The reduction reflects an expected one-time $10 billion legal accrual tied to Meta’s settlement with state attorneys general.

Excluding the charge, Post expects underlying earnings to exceed consensus estimates.

AI Investment Could Reach $205 Billion in 2027

Bank of America raised its 2027 capital expenditure forecast to $205 billion from $192 billion, exceeding Wall Street’s $195 billion estimate.

The increase reflects growing infrastructure requirements for Meta’s Muse AI products and enterprise AI initiatives.

For 2026, the analyst expects Meta to narrow its capital expenditure guidance to $135 billion-$145 billion.

Meanwhile, Bank of America expects fourth-quarter revenue of $74.1 billion and earnings of $8.74 per share, both above consensus estimates.

See More: Top Value Stocks

Muse Adoption Offers Another Growth Catalyst

Post identified Meta’s expanding AI ecosystem as a potential catalyst for the stock.

According to Sensor Tower data cited in the report, Muse surpassed 8.9 million downloads and reached 2.23 million daily active users as of Oct. 12.

The analyst believes stronger adoption, enterprise AI partnerships and improved infrastructure efficiency could support a higher valuation.

However, rising AI costs and uncertainty around monetization could pressure earnings growth in 2027.

Bank of America remains bullish, citing Meta’s advertising strength and improving AI capabilities.

Investors will focus on the company’s third-quarter results on Oct. 21 for updates on AI adoption, spending and the outlook for profitability.

Earnings and Analyst Outlook

Wall Street expects Meta to report third-quarter earnings of $6.09 per share, down from $7.25 a year earlier.

Revenue is projected to reach $63.31 billion, up from $51.24 billion in the year-ago period.

Analysts maintain a consensus Buy rating, with an average price forecast of $797.92.

Recent analyst actions include JPMorgan maintaining an Overweight rating with a $920 price forecast, Citigroup raising its forecast to $895 and Goldman Sachs maintaining a Buy rating with a $762 forecast.

Stock Analysis

Meta stock fell more than 2% on Friday as investors pulled back from major technology and growth stocks ahead of the company’s upcoming earnings report.

The Nasdaq Composite dropped 1.35%, while the S&P 500 declined 0.38%.

Meta also faces a key earnings test on Oct. 21, which could increase volatility as investors assess the company’s advertising growth and artificial intelligence spending.

Meta remains in a longer-term uptrend despite Friday’s decline.

The stock trades 9.9% above its 50-day simple moving average (SMA) and about 14% above its 200-day SMA and exponential moving average (EMA).

An October golden cross, a bullish technical signal, also supports the longer-term trend.

However, shares have slipped 2.1% below their 20-day SMA, signaling weaker short-term momentum.

The Relative Strength Index (RSI) stands at 53.11, indicating neutral momentum.

Key technical levels include resistance near $780, slightly above the stock’s 52-week high of $779.82, and support around $711.50.

PayPal Holdings, Inc. (NASDAQ:PYPL) has expanded its AI-powered commerce footprint through a partnership with Glance, an AI-powered personal shopping platform backed by InMobi.

The agentic commerce integration brings real-time product data and native checkout functionality directly to Glance consumers in the U.S.

• Where are PYPL shares going?

AI-Powered Shopping and Checkout for Consumers

Glance is embedded across more than 60 million mobile and CTV devices worldwide and provides AI-powered product discovery directly into consumers’ hands. 

Glance enables users to upload a photo to generate an AI avatar, do virtual try-ons, and share them with friends.

The integration with PayPal will enable users to discover and visualize products, build a cart, and complete their purchase without being redirected to external websites.

“The lines between where people discover, shop, and buy are disappearing,” said Mike Edmonds, vice president of Agentic Commerce at PayPal.

The partnership follows PayPal’s announcement of integrating its payment infrastructure into Meta Platforms, Inc. (NASDAQ:META) personal AI agent, Muse in September.

Enhances Benefits for Merchants

The integration provides a simple way for retailers to extend their storefronts into Glance’s platform.

PayPal’s agentic commerce services allow merchants to connect to multiple AI-powered shopping experiences through a single integration, providing real-time product pricing and availability to consumers.

Mansi Jain, COO at Glance, said that as AI-powered discovery adoption increases, the integration will allow merchants to reach consumers easily and provide them with a native in-app checkout.

Technical Analysis

PayPal is trading 5.7% above the 20-day SMA ($54.49) and 15.1% above the 200-day SMA ($50.05), keeping the intermediate uptrend intact.

The 20-day SMA sitting below the 50-day SMA ($56.10), signals a bearish alignment that can cap near-term follow-through.

MACD is above its signal line and the histogram is positive.

The bigger picture still has repair work to do after the stock’s 12-month slide of 12.81%.

The August Golden Cross (50-day SMA above the 200-day SMA) remains a longer-term tailwind.

  • Key Support: $52 — Prior demand zone that sits near key moving-average territory.

PayPal Earnings and Analyst Outlook

PayPal is scheduled to report quarterly earnings on Oct. 27.

Analysts expect earnings per share of $1.31, compared with $1.34 a year earlier. Revenue is projected to reach 8.71 billion, up from $8.42 billion.

Shopify Inc. (NASDAQ:SHOP) has reportedly increased pricing for its Grow and Advanced plans, according to JPMorgan.

The company increased the Grow plan by 13% or $10 and the Advanced plan by 20% or $60, respectively, as per a Friday note by analyst Bryan Smilek.

The firm tracks pricing changes for the U.S. merchants and the increase observed on Oct. 15 compares to prices in early October.

Smilek continues to maintain an Overweight rating with the price forecast of $200, most recently raised on Oct. 6.

• Shopify shares are sliding. Why is SHOP stock dropping?

Expects Incremental Annualized Revenue Uplift

The analyst estimates that the price increases could generate more than $40 million in incremental annualized revenue over time, assuming nearly 65% of non-Plus merchants use monthly plans and the raises are eventually rolled out globally.

Separately, previously announced Shopify Plus price increases, scheduled to take effect in 2027, could contribute over $90 million in incremental annualized Subscription Solutions revenue in 2027.

Smilek expects minimal churn risk across SMB merchants or Plus merchants due to price increase.

The firm reiterated Shopify’s significant value proposition to businesses across e-commerce enablement, Payments, and other merchant-oriented vectors.

The analysts believe the company enjoys a healthy pricing power and monetization model.

The firm though expects the company to continue to prioritize enhancing the merchant experience and capturing incremental GMV/GPV.

AI-related Cost Headwinds

The analyst estimated that AI/token consumption could drive an 180 basis points and nearly 40 basis points year-on-year headwind to the company’s 2026 Subscription and Total Gross margins.

The firm expects Plus price increases to drive high-margin MRR and help offset AI-related cost headwinds.

Analyst considers Shopify to be well-positioned as an AI beneficiary with leadership across the three layers of the agentic commerce stack: Channels, On-Platform and Infrastructure.

He highlighted the introduction of Shop Pay on Muse, through which the buyer maintains control and Shopify enabled a connector that allows merchants to manage orders, inventory and analytics directly in Muse.

The firm remains bullish on stock and raised its second-half 2026 and 2027 estimates by ~1% to 3% across Revenue, ~1% to 2% across Gross Profit, and ~1% to 2% across FCF.

Earnings and Analyst Outlook

Wall Street expects Shopify to report third-quarter earnings of 46 cents per share, up from 34 cents a year earlier.

Revenue is projected to reach $3.75 billion, up from $2.84 billion in the year-ago period.

Analysts maintain a consensus Buy rating, with an average price forecast of $171.38.

Recent analyst actions include RBC Capital maintaining an Outperform rating with a $200 price forecast on Oct. 16, Baird maintaining an Outperform rating and raising its forecast to $190 on Oct. 14 and Cantor Fitzgerald maintaining a Neutral rating with a $158 forecast on Oct. 12.

The stock is trading 9.5% above its 20-day SMA ($158.10), 15.8% above its 50-day SMA ($149.42), and 33.4% above its 200-day SMA ($129.71).

Super Micro Computer Inc. (NASDAQ:SMCI) is reshaping its finance leadership while navigating lingering accounting and governance scrutiny, even as strong AI data-center spending continues to support demand for its servers.

The stock slid almost 10% on Friday.

Super Micro Names Mark Long CFO

Super Micro appointed former Western Digital Corp. (NASDAQ:WDC) executive Mark Long as chief financial officer, effective immediately, nearly two years after beginning its search for a new finance chief.

Long replaces David Weigand, who had served as CFO since early 2021. Super Micro told Reuters on Thursday that Weigand will shift his focus toward helping "optimize and accelerate" the business but did not specify his new role.

Long previously served as Western Digital’s CFO and oversaw corporate strategy. He also co-founded technology-focused investment firm Prime Impact Capital and will report directly to CEO Charles Liang.

Accounting Scrutiny Prompted Leadership Search

Super Micro began searching for a new CFO in December 2024 following recommendations from an independent review of its accounting practices.

The review followed concerns raised by the company’s former auditor over governance, transparency and internal controls surrounding financial reporting.

Super Micro also faced scrutiny after short-seller Hindenburg Research alleged "accounting manipulation," including undisclosed related-party transactions and export-control failures. The controversy contributed to a delay in the company’s annual financial filing.

Export-Control Case Adds Another Challenge

The company has also faced legal and governance issues tied to U.S. export controls.

Most recently, Super Micro contractor Ting-Wei "Willy" Sun pleaded guilty to four counts, including conspiracy to violate U.S. export restrictions, in a scheme involving the illegal shipment of servers containing advanced NVIDIA Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA) AI chips to China.

AI Demand Supports Growth Outlook

At the Goldman Sachs Communacopia + Technology Conference, Senior Vice President of Corporate Development Michael Staiger described demand as "pretty excellent" and said the company’s roughly $60 billion order book supports its fiscal 2027 revenue outlook of $65 billion to $72 billion.

Staiger also said AI adoption is developing into a multiyear cycle, with demand broadening across neocloud, enterprise and sovereign customers. He pointed to a potential $2 trillion to $4 trillion AI infrastructure market and said "the sky’s the limit" for Super Micro over the next few years.

The company is also expanding manufacturing capacity and pushing deeper into complete AI infrastructure systems, including servers, cooling, power, storage, networking and software, which management believes can support double-digit gross margins.

The trade that carried Wall Street through much of 2026 just suffered its longest losing streak in more than two decades.

The iShares Semiconductor ETF (NASDAQ:SOXX) fell for a ninth straight session Friday, its longest skid since May 2006. The fund lost about 14% since Oct. 5 and 9.4% for the week.

The shift goes deeper than a sell-off. Investors aren’t abandoning the AI buildout, but they’re asking a question that has taken a back seat for months: Who pays for it?

The Rhyme With Today is the Cost of Money

The Federal Reserve raised rates to 5.00% on May 10, 2006. At the time, it was the sixteenth straight hike, and investors sold emerging-market equities alongside commodities.

The semiconductor sector, a favorite the prior year, was among the first to crack.

Fast forward to 2026: The Fed lifted rates to 3.75%-4.00% in September. The 10-year Treasury yield sat at about 5.09% on Friday, Oct. 16, after touching 5.37% last week.

The Credit Channel

September consumer prices rose 3.7% from a year earlier, above the 3.6% expected, while the producer price index climbed 6.3%, a four-year high.

Odds of an October hike jumped to nearly 50% after the CPI report, then eased to about 17% by Friday morning, according to CME FedWatch.

If memory is the plumbing of artificial intelligence, CoreWeave Inc. (NASDAQ:CRWV)’s bonds are the water bill.

The cloud provider fell 15.5% on Wednesday as the cost of insuring its debt hit a record, and its 9% notes slid to about 80 cents on the dollar, yielding more than 15%.

CoreWeave’s credit default swaps, which insurance investors buy to hedge against default, jumped past 1,000 basis points. This implies roughly a 60% chance of default within five years.

Among the Worst Nasdaq 100 Performers Over 5 Days:

  • CoreWeave Inc. (NASDAQ:CRWV) fell 25.75%
  • Rocket Lab Corp. (NASDAQ:RKLB) at 25.06%
  • Nebius Group N.V. (NASDAQ:NBIS) at 24.58%
  • Lumentum Holdings Inc. (NASDAQ:LITE) at 24.16%.
  • Palo Alto Networks Inc. (NASDAQ:PANW) lost 18.32% and
  • CrowdStrike Holdings Inc. (NASDAQ:CRWD) 17.37%.

Inside the iShares Semiconductor ETF:

  • Cerebras Systems Inc. (NASDAQ:CBRS) dropped 21.41%
  • Credo Technology Group Holding Ltd (NASDAQ:CRDO) 20.81% and
  • MACOM Technology Solutions Holdings Inc. (NASDAQ:MTSI) 19.94%.
  • Applied Materials Inc. (NASDAQ:AMAT), Teradyne Inc. (NASDAQ:TER) and Lam Research Corp. (NASDAQ:LRCX) each fell 16% to 18%.
  • Micron Technology Inc. (NASDAQ:MU) fell 13.18% and
  • Sandisk Corp. (NASDAQ:SNDK) 16.12%

Every holding shown in the Roundhill Memory ETF (NYSE:DRAM) finished lower, and optical names fell the most since the dot-com bust. But the sharpest moves came in the networking hardware that wires AI data centers together:

  • Coherent Corp. (NYSE:COHR) plunged 24.8%, its biggest one-day drop since March 31, 2000.
  • Ciena Corp. (NYSE:CIEN) fell 25.02%, its worst day since September 2008.

Korea’s Worst Week Since Lehman

South Korea’s KOSPI fell 14.46% this week, its worst weekly drop since October 2008, when it lost 20.5% after Lehman Brothers collapsed.

Even the March 2020 crash never produced a weekly loss that large.

Thursday alone brought a 7.57% plunge and a 20-minute trading halt.

SK Hynix Inc. (NASDAQ:SKHY) lost 24.3% on the week and Samsung Electronics Co. Ltd. (OTC:SSNLF) 17.8%, both their worst weeks since 2008.

Bank Of America Sees A Cisco Echo

Bank of America analyst Vivek Arya reached for a different dot-com analogy in a Friday client note.

Nvidia Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA), Broadcom Inc. (NASDAQ:AVGO) and Micron trade at about 13 times forward earnings on average, inside the 10-to-20 range where Cisco Systems Inc. (NASDAQ:CSCO) changed hands after its bubble burst.

"Investors are paying post-crash multiples for a cycle that hasn’t crashed," Arya said.

Cisco peaked at $82 in March 2000, fell to $8.12 by October 2002 and did not reclaim its high until March 2026. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index now sits about 22% below its June 22 record, its second bear market this year.

Money did not leave the market. It moved.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average gained about 1.4% this week while the Nasdaq 100 lost nearly 4% and the S&P 500 about 0.8%, and the 10-year yield fell about 15 basis points as investors sought bonds.

Meta Platform, Inc’s (NASDAQ:META) Oct. 21 earnings report could offer a critical test of whether artificial intelligence investments are translating into stronger profits, with implications for ETFs holding the social media giant.

Bank of America expects Meta to report third-quarter revenue of $63.8 billion, above the $63.3 billion consensus estimate. The bank also forecasts fourth-quarter revenue of $74.1 billion, ahead of the $73.6 billion market estimate, as AI-driven improvements in advertising support growth.

But the spending required to sustain that growth could complicate the outlook for technology-heavy ETFs.

The bigger concern is the scale of Meta’s AI infrastructure spending. Bank of America expects 2026 capital expenditure of $140 billion to $145 billion and projects it could reach $205 billion in 2027. Investors will be looking for evidence that stronger advertising returns can justify those costs.

• Meta Platforms stock is taking a hit today. What’s pressuring META stock?

Three ETFs to watch

Meta exposure across selected funds:

First Trust Dow Jones Internet ETF (NYSE:FDN): With a portfolio weight of 11.04% toward Meta

Roundhill Magnificent Seven ETF (BATS:MAGS): With a portfolio weight of 14.26% toward Meta

Invesco QQQ Trust (NASDAQ:QQQ): With a portfolio weight of 3.37% toward Meta

MAGS offers exposure to the Magnificent Seven stocks, making Meta’s earnings particularly relevant to the fund’s performance. A strong advertising outlook could reinforce investor confidence in the group’s AI monetization potential, while concerns about rising infrastructure costs could weigh on sentiment toward these mega-cap technology stocks.

FDN provides more concentrated exposure to internet businesses, including companies whose revenues depend on digital advertising and online engagement. Meta’s results could therefore influence sentiment toward the broader internet sector, particularly if management provides fresh evidence that AI is improving advertising efficiency and monetization.

QQQ, meanwhile, tracks the Nasdaq-100 Index and offers broader exposure across major non-financial Nasdaq-listed companies. Although Meta accounts for a smaller 3.37% of its portfolio, its earnings could still affect the fund through its direct stock exposure and the broader implications for AI-related investment and technology valuations.

The distinction matters for investors. MAGS has the greatest direct sensitivity to Meta among these three funds based on the supplied weights, FDN offers a more focused internet-sector angle, and QQQ provides broader technology and growth-stock exposure. However, actual performance will also depend on how other portfolio holdings perform and how markets interpret Meta’s results.

See More: Top Growth Stocks

The Earnings Risk for ETF Investors

Meta’s earnings-per-share figure may also require careful interpretation. Bank of America expects $3.79, against the $6.08 consensus, partly because of a one-off $10 billion legal settlement charge. The bank expects operating income to exceed market expectations after excluding that charge.

For ETF investors, the key signals will be fourth-quarter revenue guidance, evidence that AI is improving ad targeting and engagement, and management’s outlook for infrastructure spending. A stronger advertising outlook could reinforce the AI growth narrative, but accelerating costs without corresponding revenue gains could pressure valuations across technology-heavy portfolios.

President Donald Trump’s White House ballroom project donor list reportedly reveals companies and individuals linked to federal contracts, policy decisions, and a presidential pardon.

NVIDIA Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA) and Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL) each pledged $25 million, matching contributions from the Adelson family and telecommunications billionaire Charles Ergen, reported the Washington Post on Thursday.

Alphabet Inc.‘s Google (NASDAQ:GOOGL) (NASDAQ:GOOG) committed $22 million through the John P. Coale Esq. trust. Microsoft Corp. (NASDAQ:MSFT) and Palantir Technologies Inc. (NASDAQ:PLTR) committed $10 million, each, as per the list.

“The donors for the White House ballroom project represent a wide array of great American companies and generous individuals, all of whom are contributing to make the People’s House better for generations to come," White House Spokesman Davis Ingle told Benzinga in an emailed statement.

However, Ingle noted that the “White House does not discuss or disclose personal information about individuals’ private donations they may or may not have been given to nonprofit organizations.”

“As an American company, our support for the U.S. is paramount, and independent of any business interests. We were proud to be able to make a donation to a nonpartisan trust that serves all Americans and have said so publicly since the donation was made,” an Nvidia spokesperson told Benzinga.

The private fundraising campaign collected $333 million, including at least $77 million from anonymous donors, based on internal records reviewed by The Post. The documents identify 57 donors who pledged at least $100,000, the report added.

Isabela Herrera, daughter of  Venezuelan-Italian international banker Julio Herrera Velutini, pledged $2.5 million to Trump’s White House ballroom in September 2025, months after Velutini’s bribery charges were reduced. She paid $835,000 in October, and Trump pardoned her father in January 2026, the report stated.

Contributions flow through a nonprofit before being transferred to the government and a White House account controlled directly by Trump.

Microsoft, Google and Palantir did not immediately respond to Benzinga’s request for comments.

Ballroom Project Faced Legal Challenges

The fundraising disclosures add detail to a project that has faced political and legal scrutiny. On Aug. 31, the Supreme Court’s ruling allowed construction of the White House ballroom and military complex to proceed, with Trump targeting completion in 2028. The President said the ballroom project is funded entirely by private donors and corporations, with no cost to taxpayers, and stated that the construction is under budget and ahead of schedule.

Despite top tech firms and corporations contributing to the project, JPMorgan Chase & Co. (NYSE:JPM) CEO Jamie Dimon said in November last year that the bank is “quite conscious of risks” and would not donate to Trump’s White House ballroom project, citing concerns that contributions could be perceived as “buying” political favors or invite scrutiny from future administrations and the Justice Department.

Nvidia Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA) CEO Jensen Huang detailed how repeated unanswered calls and a personal letter helped create the company’s decades-long relationship with Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. (NYSE:TSM).

Huang recounted the story on Wednesday, during a vlog in Taiwan with podcaster Lex Fridman. In the late 1990s, Nvidia needed a manufacturer for its graphics chips, but foundry capacity was limited. Huang located TSMC’s U.S. office in the Yellow Pages and called repeatedly.

"Nobody called me. Nobody called me back," Huang said. He eventually sent TSMC founder Morris Chang a lengthy letter seeking help.

Chang later contacted Huang and invited him to Taiwan. “Maybe we won’t have to die,” Huang said, thrilled that the TSMC CEO ultimately responded.

Huang visited TSMC and rival United Microelectronics Corp. (NYSE:UMC), saying both companies impressed him before Chang’s focus on integrity, governance and long-term partnerships won Nvidia’s business.

Chang assured Jensen that his company would go to great lengths to support a potential partnership. “For the whole time, 30 years, they’ve been jumping through hoops for us,” Huang told Friedman.

In a March Lex Fridman podcast, Huang confirmed that TSMC founder Morris Chang even offered him the chance to lead the chipmaker in 2013. Huang said he was deeply honored by the offer but declined because he was committed to Nvidia’s long-term vision and believed the company’s potential impact was too important to walk away from.

“And so I declined it, not because it wasn’t an incredible offer. It’s an unbelievable offer, but I simply couldn’t take it,” Huang said.

Read Also: NVDA-Led AI Boom Looks a Lot Like the Railroad Bubble of 1873, Pulitzer-Winning Historian Warns

How TSMC Helped Save Nvidia From Collapse

The relationship emerged when Nvidia faced severe financial pressure. A previous account of Huang’s letter, described by Morris Chang, indicated that Nvidia was near bankruptcy before the partnership helped redirect its trajectory.

“We were a billion-dollar company at that time, and to be a major customer of ours, he would have to produce revenue for us of at least $50 million a year,” Chang said. Nvidia’s chip’s success helped Huang avert financial collapse and establish the company as a leader in gaming and graphics, making it one of TSMC’s top five customers within two to three years.

The partnership later became strategically important as Nvidia moved from graphics processors into AI hardware. In November 2025, Huang praised TSMC’s support for Blackwell chip production amid what he called "very strong demand."

TSMC Revenue Jumps 41% on AI Demand

Huang’s comments came in a day before TSMC reported third-quarter revenue of $46.72 billion, up 41.2% year over year and 16.2% sequentially, beating analyst estimates of $45.62 billion. TSMC posted a 66.4% gross margin, a 58.7% operating margin and a 51.1% net profit margin.

Advanced technologies of 7-nanometer and below accounted for 79% of wafer revenue, with 2-nm technology contributing 8%, 3-nm 33%, 5-nm 28%, and 7-nm 10%.

Robotics remains in a "Lego era," with actuators, robotic hands, software, and safety standards still being rebuilt, and not on the cusp of a ChatGPT moment even as capital floods into AI. Amulya Vishwanath, founder of Techable VC and a former NVIDIA Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA) product marketing leader, made the case on TechCrunch’s Equity podcast that aired on Friday.

Vishwanath spent seven years leading product marketing for Nvidia’s robotics platforms. She also worked on the company’s Isaac Lab and the GR00T humanoid effort.

Simulation, Safety Seen as Next Catalysts

"There’s been quite a bit of progress. But that said, there’s a Lego era that’s happening for robotics," she said, adding that simulation will grow more critical.

Vishwanath said the industry needs "more emphasis on open-source safety and newer standards" that need to be set for robotics. Large companies now partner with startups and universities, she added, citing a possible tie-up among NVIDIA, a university, startups and companies.

Early Money Goes to the Building Blocks

That view shapes where Vishwanath invests. Her firm backs early-stage startups in robotics, materials science and life sciences, where the foundational pieces are still being built.

Views differ on how close deployment is. Ouster Inc. (NASDAQ:OUST) CEO Angus Pacala told Benzinga in August that mature pilots are moving into production, but the key question is whether robots can work safely every day for years.

A September Citrini Research report found most humanoid robots remain in development, training or tele-operated demos, with real-world deployments closer to pilots than clear return-on-investment cases.

That gap explains her focus on components. Vishwanath said U.S. startups are now making actuators, robotic hands and U.S.-made robots, and she called a domestic supply chain important.

Actuators act as a robot’s muscles, and a single humanoid needs dozens.

Chamath Palihapitiya warns that a 10-year bond yield of 5.5% to 6% would “run over” any business reliant on financing spreads, no matter what it does, including AI businesses.

The venture capitalist made the remarks on an episode of the All-In Podcast that aired on Friday. He said the risk has nothing to do with AI. He tied it to debt-to-GDP levels and other factors across broad-based Western economies.

Deficits Seen as the Pressure Valve

Palihapitiya said that as long as the 10-year yield is kept from reaching those levels, "we’re going to be fine."

The Sri Lanka-born Canadian-American entrepreneur said policymakers must focus on deficits and find a "fair trade" where the bond market backs off to "keep the party going" after the midterms.

Huge spending proposals, he warned, would push the 10-year higher and set off a "negative cascade" to everything. A calmer approach focused on cutting waste, he said, would draw a favorable response.

Why Financing Spreads Matter

A financing spread is the premium a borrower pays over a benchmark rate, often the risk-free rate, which is the return on a safe government bond. When the 10-year yield rises, the benchmark cost of capital can rise for businesses whose financing is priced off longer-term rates.

He also called the exposure an Achilles’ heel, a single weak point in an otherwise strong system. He said "all this other stuff is complete goodness," but financing these businesses as a spread over the risk-free rate is "the big problem."

The 10-year Treasury yield recently touched 5.34%, its highest level since 2002. In early October, JPMorgan Chase & Co. (NYSE:JPM) CEO Jamie Dimon said that AI spending is competing with government borrowing for capital.

Goldman Sachs Group Inc. (NYSE:GS) CEO David Solomon raised a related concern earlier this week, saying AI infrastructure financing could pressure borrowing costs and threaten some projects. The 10-year Treasury yield has risen about 75 basis points since early July.

Big Tech Seen as the Backstop

Because of that risk, Palihapitiya said, large technology companies would need to step in during a worst-case scenario. He named Microsoft Corp. (NASDAQ:MSFT), Alphabet Inc. (NASDAQ:GOOG) (NASDAQ:GOOGL), Meta Platforms Inc. (NASDAQ:META) and Nvidia Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA).

Chamath said large technology companies such as Microsoft, Alphabet, Meta and Nvidia would need to step in if the sector faced a one- or two-year correction.

The S&P 500, Nasdaq 100 and Dow Jones Industrial Average have pulled back modestly from their highs for the year, even as corporate earnings growth continued and the artificial intelligence (AI) boom cooled.

The Nasdaq 100 fell to 29,187, down 6.9% from its highest point this month and its lowest level since September 16. Similarly, the S&P 500 dropped to 7,660, down 2.42% from its high for the year. The Dow Jones Industrial Average traded at 52,000, a modest decline from this year’s high of 54,757.

US Stocks to React to Top Corporate Earnings

The S&P 500, Dow Jones and Nasdaq 100 indices will react to several notable corporate earnings, continuing a process that started last week. SpaceX (NASDAQ:SPCX), GE Aerospace (NYSE:GE), and Netflix (NASDAQ:NFLX) will release their numbers on Tuesday, while Meta Platforms (NASDAQ:META) and Tesla (NASDAQ:TSLA) will publish their numbers on Wednesday.

FactSet (NYSE:FDS) data shows that 9% of S&P 500 companies have reported their results so far, with blended earnings growth at 29%. If that holds as the final figure, it will mark the third consecutive quarter of earnings growth above 25%. Strong earnings growth will likely lift the stock market.

Read Also: Nebius Stock Falls After Key Gartner Warning as Short Interest Nears 20%

Rising Crude Oil Prices

US stocks will also react to the rising crude oil prices. Brent touched the important resistance level of $110 on Friday, while the West Texas Intermediate (WTI) rose to $101. This rally has led to a surge in gasoline and diesel prices, with the latter trading at the highest level on record.

Rising crude oil prices have an impact on the stock market. For one, oil and gas companies like ExxonMobil (NYSE:XOM) and Chevron (NYSE:CVX) benefit as their revenue and profits jump. 

On the other hand, it leads to higher inflation, which pushes the Federal Reserve to hike interest rates. Data released last week showed that the headline and core consumer prices rose 3.7% and 2.6%, respectively, moving further away from the Fed’s 2% target. These dynamics also push bond yields higher, which affects stocks.

AI Bubble Jitters

The S&P 500, Nasdaq 100, and Dow Jones will also react to the ongoing jitters in the artificial intelligence industry. Last week, most companies in the sector, including Nvidia, Micron, SanDisk, and AMD, fell as warnings about the industry grew louder.

One of the headlines was that Anthropic’s third-quarter revenue grew at a slower pace than expected. OpenAI’s annualized revenue was $20 billion lower than initially reported by prominent media companies. 

At the same time, bond yields of top AI companies like CoreWeave and Oracle continued rising, while Gartner warned of substantial impairments of AI infrastructure by 2030. Firmus, an Australian data center company, also cancelled its IPO as investors pushed back against its valuation. Similar headlines will likely push US stocks lower.

Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) stock has slipped into a technical correction as the AI Bubble Index climbs to an extreme level. After hitting a record high of $243 earlier this month, the shares have fallen 12.2% to $214. The pullback could continue, since the stock has also formed a rising wedge pattern.

AI Bubble Index is Rising

Top analysts have been warning about the artificial intelligence bubble. In a statement last week, David Rosenberg warned that the bubble may burst as soon as next year, leading to a US recession.

Ray Dalio, Bridgewater Associates’ founder, has constantly warned that the bubble may burst soon as US bond yields continue rising. Indeed, the closely watched ten-year bond yield jumped to a two-decade high of 5.3%.

These warnings come at a time the AI Stock Bubble Index has jumped to the elevated level of 74. If the trend continues, it may enter the extreme zone of 80 as soon as this week.

This index looks at six measures, with valuation having the biggest weight of 25%. The other measures it looks at are private capital velocity and valuation expansion, gap between AI investment and disclosed revenue, and media and search attention. 

Read Also: Broadcom Stock Is Down 35% From Its Peak as AI Bubble Warnings Rise, but Analysts Stay Optimistic

It also looks at market concentration, which looks at how AI equity performance depends on a narrow group of companies, and the scale of AI compute compared to near-term monetization.

Nvidia would be highly exposed if the AI bubble bursts. It is the biggest supplier of GPUs that power the AI industry. It is also a big investor in companies across all areas of the AI industry, including neoclouds, optics and photonics, and AI labs like OpenAI and Anthropic. 

On the positive side, Nvidia’s business has continued growing. Its last earnings report showed that its revenue jumped to over $104 billion in the second quarter. Jensen Huang also hinted that the annual revenue will jump by over 70% next year, much higher than expected.

Nvidia is also highly undervalued, with its forward price-to-earnings ratio of 22 being much lower than the five-year average of 42. This explains why the company recently announced a $150 billion share buyback.

Nvidia Stock Formed a Rising Wedge Pattern

The ongoing NVDA stock retreat happened after it formed a rising wedge pattern, which is made up of two rising and converging trendlines. The breakdown happened as the two lines neared their convergence.

Nvidia has dropped below the 50-day Exponential Moving Average (EMA), while the Supertrend indicator has turned red. Therefore, the most likely outlook is bearish, with the initial target being at $209, its lowest level on September 14. A drop below that level will point to more downside to $200.

GE Aerospace (NYSE:GE) stock has slumped 20% from its high for the year, erasing billions of dollars in market value. It was trading at $313, well below its August peak of $388, and an impending death cross suggests more downside ahead.

GE Aerospace Stock Has Dived Ahead of Earnings

The ongoing GE stock decline has coincided with that of its competitors. RTX Corporation (NYSE:RTX), which owns Pratt & Whitney, has dropped by 14% from its peak this year. In the UK, Rolls-Royce Holdings has fallen by 15%, while in France, Safran has dropped by 13%.

GE Aerospace will be in the spotlight this week as it releases its earnings report, which is expected to show that its growth continued. Benzinga data shows that analysts expect the upcoming results to show that its revenue rose 14% to $12.88 billion in the third quarter. 

Read Also: Dow Jones, Nasdaq 100, S&P 500 Outlook: Top Catalysts to Move US Stocks This Week

Its guidance for the year is that its revenue will hit $50.3 billion, up by 19% from the $42.2 billion it made last year. This growth is being driven by the rising product and service orders from the biggest airlines in the world. 

The most recent results showed that GE Aerospace received orders worth $16.5 billion in the second quarter, up by 17% YoY. This increase brought its backlog to $210 billion, and management expects the growth to continue. 

The challenge, however, is that GE Aerospace is highly overvalued. It has a forward price-to-earnings ratio of 40, much higher than the manufacturing sector median of 19. These multiples are higher than other fast-growing companies like Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA), Micron (NASDAQ:MU), and Lumentum (NASDAQ:LITE).

Wall Street analysts expect GE Aerospace’s stock to have more upside. Wells Fargo sees it rising to $380, while Jefferies predicts a jump to $435. Deutsche Bank has a target of $450, and Goldman Sachs expects the stock to reach $410.

GE Stock May Drop Further in the Near Term

Technicals suggest that the GE stock price may drop further in the near future. It formed a double-top pattern with a neckline of $335, its lowest level on July 16 this year.

The stock has dropped to the 61.8% Fibonacci Retracement level. Worse, GE is about to form a death cross pattern as the spread between the 50-day and 200-day moving averages has narrowed to just 5 points. A death cross would point to more downside over time. 

If a bearish breakout occurs, the first target to watch is $296, the lowest level on October 8. A drop below that level would point to more downside toward the 78.6% retracement at $294. On the flip side, a move above the resistance at $328, the 50% retracement level, would invalidate the bearish outlook.

U.S. stock futures were higher late Sunday, signaling a bounce from Friday’s slide in the Nasdaq Composite, even as calls for a Black Monday crash were trending.

The Fear Is ‘Overdone’

The Kobeissi Letter took the opposite approach to the calls for a Black Monday crash, posting on X a chart that tracks every time the term has trended since May 2025.

Over that stretch, the S&P 500 has climbed from about 5,500 to around 7,650, and the market commentator called the selloff worries “overdone.”

In an analysis published last week, the firm argued that the S&P 500 is in a “stealth” bear market “within a bull market.”

It said that 84% of the index’s stocks trade at least 10% below their record highs, while just 10 stocks have driven 70% of its gain since the March low.

Without the Iran war, the index could, it contends, be above 9,000.

Read Also: 'This Is What I Will Be Doing’: Elon Musk Says He’ll Give Shares To The Public After Anthropic Announces 5% Fund

Futures Move Higher

S&P 500 futures rose 0.72% to 7,760 on Sunday, after the index closed 1.09% lower at 7,659.44 on Friday. Nasdaq 100 futures gained 1.2% to 29,743 and Dow futures added 0.44% to 52,446.

On Friday, the Nasdaq Composite closed 2.14% lower at 26,140.03, and the Dow fell 0.34%.

Memory stocks were under pressure last week with investors balancing strong AI-driven demand against rising interest rates, Chinese competition and uncertainty over how long supply shortages will last.

In Asia, South Korea’s benchmark index KOSPI rose 0.61%, while Japan’s Nikkei 225 fell 0.88%.

Recession Odds Split

Traders on the Polygon (CRYPTO: POL)-based Polymarket have priced in a 7% chance of a U.S. recession by the end of 2026, with a 35% chance of a recession by the end of 2027.

Rosenberg Research founder David Rosenberg said last week that he sees better-than-even odds of a recession within a year, calling the market a bubble driven by investor behavior.

BlackRock Inc. CEO Larry Fink cautioned that local moratoriums on data center construction could tip the U.S. economy into a recession by disrupting the capital spending driving growth.
